meaning: He who is like the ibis

phonemes.desc: Palatalized voiced alveolar stop [ɟ] or affricate, written with d-dot-below; the first consonant of Ḏḥwtj
Voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ], the dotted h that follows the palatal d
Bilabial glide [w], represented in writing by the quail-chick sign
Final consonants t-y, with the y indicating a palatalization or the Greek ending -is

pronunciation.approximation: tji-HOO-tee — the first consonant is like a 'dj' made against the hard palate, and the middle h is a dry throat-fricative.

pronunciation.note: Ḏḥwtj is Tier-1: the underdotted ḏ and ḥ are distinctive letters the ASCII form loses. Egyptian writing records only the consonants ḏ-ḥ-w-tj; the vowels are reconstructed from Coptic and Greek sources. The initial palatal ḏ and the pharyngeal ḥ are both non-English sounds preserved in the Unicode form.

domains.title: Lord of the Sacred Word
domains.subtitle: Writing, Wisdom, Moon, and Judgment
domains.lead: Ḏḥwtj is the ibis-headed scribe of the gods, the measurer of time, the reckoner of accounts, and the moon whose light lets humans see at night. He invented writing, preserved the laws of Maat, and stands beside Osiris in the Hall of Judgment to record the verdict of the heart. Where Ptḥ creates by speaking, Thoth creates by writing: he is the god who makes knowledge durable.

cards.name: Moon and Measurement
cards.desc: Thoth is the moon that measures months, festivals, and the night hours of the Duat.

cards.name: Scribe of Maat
cards.desc: He records the weighing of the heart and knows the spells that protect the justified dead.

cards.name: Mediator and Healer
cards.desc: He intervenes in disputes among gods, restores the Eye of Horus, and masters medicine and magic.

cards.name: Hermopolis
cards.desc: His city Khemenu, 'Eight-Town,' was a center of learning and the cult of the Ogdoad.

symbols.name: Ibis

symbols.name: Baboon
symbols.meaning: Thoth's other sacred animal, associated with the dawn and the rising moon

symbols.name: Scribal palette and reed pens
symbols.meaning: The tools of the divine scribe who records all deeds and spells

symbols.name: Crescent moon and disk
symbols.meaning: The lunar phases by which Thoth measures time and renews the cosmic order

symbols.name: Eye of Horus (wedjat)
symbols.meaning: Restored by Thoth after the conflict of Horus and Seth, symbolizing wholeness regained

mythology.lead: Thoth moves through Egyptian myth as the indispensable companion: he is present at creation, mediates divine quarrels, heals the wounded eye, and judges the dead. His stories are less about his own ambition than about the power of knowledge, writing, and measured speech to resolve conflict and preserve order.

myths.title: The Word That Organized Creation
myths.text: Egyptian creation had many authors — Atum of Heliopolis, Ptḥ of Memphis, the eight of Hermopolis — and Ḏḥwtj is the one indispensable technician in all of them. The Shabaka Stone's Memphite Theology makes him effectively the tongue of Ptḥ: the creator conceives in his heart, and it is Thoth's word that carries the conception into speech, 'which created all that exists.' Elsewhere he is credited with inventing hieroglyphs, numbers, and the calendar — the tools by which humans keep Maat on earth — and the Hermopolitan cosmogony makes his own city, Khemenu, the mound that first rose from the flood. Creation, in this theology, is not only a making but a record: nothing made is secure until it is written. The myth means speech without a scribe is unfinished creation — the word that is not written down has not yet fully happened.

myths.title: The Mediator of the Gods
myths.text: In the New Kingdom narrative The Contendings of Horus and Set (Papyrus Chester Beatty I), Ḏḥwtj is the divine institution that keeps the brawl from becoming apocalypse: he is scribe to the Ennead's tribunal, messenger between the courts above and below, and healer of both combatants — restoring Horus's torn eye and Set's injured testicles with the same professional calm. When the gods deadlock for years, it is Thoth who carries the correspondence with Osiris in the Duat, and Thoth who records the final verdict that seats Horus on the throne. His prestige is the point: the text is a comedy in which kings, warriors, and even the sun's council behave like litigants, and only the scribe behaves like a god. The myth defines a specific kind of sacredness: not the hand that throws the spear but the hand that writes the verdict — the power that ends wars by making decisions legible.

myths.title: The Scribe of the Weighing
myths.text: Spell 125 of the Book of the Dead gives Ḏḥwtj his most solemn office. In the Hall of the Two Truths he stands beside the scales where ꜣnpw weighs the heart against the feather of Maat, and it is Thoth who reads the balance and writes the record — the divine audit trail on which every verdict of Osiris rests. 'Thoth, exact of voice, the scribe of the gods' is his title there; the justified dead are those whose entry his pen admits. The deceased, knowing this, did not merely submit to the judgment — they tried to become it: funerary texts of the New Kingdom let the dead declare 'I am Thoth,' claiming the protection of the sacred words for their own case. The myth means the afterlife is a bureaucracy staffed by the wise: survive the weighing, and it is because the god of writing has written you down among the living forever.

myths.title: Winning the Days from the Moon
myths.text: Plutarch (On Isis and Osiris 12) preserves the calendar myth in which Ḏḥwtj outwits time itself. When Rē cursed the sky-goddess Nut that she should bear children 'on no day of the year,' Thoth — gambler and reckoner, the moon's own accountant — played draughts with the moon-god and won a seventy-second part of the moon's light, five full days outside the calendar. On them Nut bore her five children: Osiris, Horus the Elder, Set, Isis, Nephthys — the entire cast of Egypt's central drama, born on borrowed time. The five epagomenal days, 'the five days upon the year,' were celebrated across Egypt as the gods' birthdays, and Egypt's 365-day year balanced on this ancient gift. The myth makes the calendar itself a story: the year has no room for the future until the god of writing cheats the arithmetic.

myths.title: Bringing Back the Eye
myths.text: The 'Myth of the Eye of the Sun,' known from copies such as Papyrus Leiden I 384 and temple versions at Kom Ombo and Dendera, sends Ḏḥwtj on his most delicate embassy. The Eye of Rē — the furious lioness who stormed away to Nubia in rage — must be coaxed home, for without her the land withers. Rē sends the cleverest speaker he has: Thoth, who finds the goddess ravening in the desert and does not fight her but talks — flatteries, fables, gentle jokes — until her anger softens, her lioness skin is shed, and she consents to return as the mild, life-giving Eye. Wherever the myth is told, the divine council agrees that no other god could have managed it: not force, not magic, but speech. The myth praises a specific genius: there are disasters that power cannot retrieve — only a perfect speech can bring the light back home.

lore.syncretism: Thoth's most enduring syncretism is with the Greek Hermes, producing Hermes Trismegistus, 'Thrice-Great Hermes,' the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus. This Graeco-Egyptian figure became a cornerstone of late antique mysticism, alchemy, and astrology, and was reclaimed by Renaissance humanists such as Ficino and Pico della Mirandola. In Coptic Egypt, Thoth's month name (Thōout) survived in the Christian calendar. His ibis and baboon forms influenced medieval bestiaries and early modern emblem books.
lore.culturalLegacy: Thoth lives on as the patron of writers, scholars, librarians, and occultists. The figure of Hermes Trismegistus shaped Western esotericism for nearly two millennia, and the word 'hermetic' still signals sealed, secret knowledge. In popular culture, Thoth appears as a wise moon-god, a keeper of arcane books, and a judge of souls. For Egyptologists, he embodies the Egyptian conviction that writing is a form of magic: the right words, properly recorded, can preserve a person beyond death.
lore.extendedMeditation: Thoth is the god who believes that what is written endures. In a world of disappearing messages and ephemeral speech, he reminds us that some words must be preserved: laws, treaties, poems, names. To invoke Thoth is to take seriously the responsibility of the scribe — the one who decides what gets remembered and how. His moonlight is not the blazing sun of Ra but the softer light by which we read, measure, and think.

lore.archaeology: Thoth's principal cult center was Khemenu (Hermopolis Magna) in Middle Egypt, where remains of his temple and the nearby ibis and baboon cemeteries have been excavated. Thousands of mummified ibises and baboons were deposited as votive offerings at Saqqara, Tuna el-Gebel, and other sites. Temple reliefs from the New Kingdom onward show Thoth as scribe, healer, and lunar measurer. The Graeco-Roman Hermetic texts and Coptic references preserve his later reputation as Hermes Trismegistus.
